summary: Gives a scenario for using the Network Journal: users mail messages or whole files to the NIC using SNDMSG or their site's mail, and the NIC converts them to NLS files, journalizes them and sends them to recipients.

eli5.summary: You mail a note to the NIC. It files the note in a shared notebook and passes copies to the people you chose.

questions: how to use the network journal
how did you send mail through the arpanet
subtitle: A way to mail messages and files through the ARPANET and have them journalized.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET had separate tools for sending mail and sharing documents, making it cumbersome to send a message to multiple recipients or archive it for group reference.
tldr.mechanism: Users send mail to a special NIC address with a slash-separated list of recipient names. The NIC converts the message into an NLS file, assigns it a journal number and sends it to each recipient. Recipients retrieve their messages via FTP using the journal number.
tldr.outcome: Short messages come directly to recipients, while longer ones are stored with a reference number that anyone can retrieve later, creating a shared message log.

today: The Network Journal was an early collaborative messaging system on the ARPANET. It was later superseded by modern email systems and shared document repositories, but it pioneered the idea of journalized, retrievable messages.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Network Journal is a service offered by the Network Information Center that accepts mail messages and complete files from ARPANET users. The NIC converts these submissions into NLS files, assigns each a journal number, and distributes them to specified recipients. This RFC describes the procedure for sending messages and files through the Network Journal and retrieving them.
sections.eli5: It is a mailbox system where you send a message to the NIC and it files and forwards it to others.

sections.title: Sending Messages via SNDMSG
sections.content: A user sends a message by using the SNDMSG command with a specially formatted address. The format is sender-ident/recipient-ident(s)@NIC, for example JEW/DHC@NIC. Multiple recipients can be specified, and the sender can also include regular ARPANET addresses after a comma to send the same message via normal mail. The message can include plain text or reference an entire file inserted with the ^B command.
sections.eli5: You type a special mail command with the sender's name and recipients' names separated by a slash, and send it to the NIC.

sections.title: Retrieving Files from the Network Journal
sections.content: Recipients receive a citation such as <GJOURNAL>21695 that identifies their message in the NIC's journal. They retrieve the actual file by using FTP to connect to the NIC, logging in as ANONYMOUS with password NIC, and using the GET command with the citation reference. Alternative retrieval methods include TELNET with the MAIL command or direct FTP file transfer, each with similar steps for different system types.
sections.eli5: You get back a number like 21695, then use FTP to download the actual message from the NIC by that number.
